title: A Smile for the Choir
premise: Odile Crane hosts the graveyard shift at KRVL, a dying AM station, where her late-night callers include the recently dead—people who died within the past week, calling in to finish unfinished business. When an excavation crew beneath the old Aldermoor Chapel unearths a door sealed from the inside, the calls stop being gentle and start being demands: something got out, and it is wearing the voices of her listeners. Odile discovers that in 1974 the chapel choir vanished mid-broadcast, taken by whatever the congregation had bargained with to survive a fire—and that her own mother was the soloist who escaped. To end it, Odile must return what was taken: not an object, but the choir's final song, sung back through the door by someone willing to stay on the other side. In the end she gives them the song, seals the door from the inside as they once did, and survives only because her mother's voice, kept all these years on a reel-to-reel tape, answers for her.
about_author: Cyrus Dravenmoor spent a decade as an overnight radio operator in small-market stations across the Rust Belt, collecting the strange calls and dead air that haunt his fiction. He writes horror about institutions—churches, stations, hospitals—that outlive the people they were built to protect.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. We meet her ritualized night: lights counted, doors checked, calls screened. A woman phones in to thank Odile for playing her wedding song—then mentions her funeral, held Tuesday. The beat is quiet unease; Odile's rules keep the dead polite, and tonight one of them breaks a rule gently.

chapters.title: The Counting House
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Flashback woven into present: how the calls started after her mother's death, and why Odile counts doors—her mother taught her that thresholds remember. A second caller, a drowned boy, asks if the door under the chapel is open yet. She doesn't know what he means. Beat: dread arriving sideways.

chapters.title: Excavation
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The city crew digging the chapel foundation for a parking garage hits a stone door, sealed from the inside, warm to the touch. Odile broadcasts live from the site; the foreman hears singing under the ground. That night every caller is silent except for breathing in unison. Beat: the story's engine starts.

chapters.title: Voices on Loan
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The dead callers change—they speak in unison now, politely demanding she 'bring it back.' Her producer Marcus thinks she's cracking; she plays him a recording of a caller who died before the show aired. Beat: isolation deepens; the supernatural becomes undeniable but unshareable.

chapters.title: What Mother Kept
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, moving through her mother's storage unit. She finds reel-to-reel tapes labeled 1974, a choir robe with a scorched hem, and a hymnal with pages torn out—the final song removed. A note in her mother's hand: 'Never sing along.' Beat: inheritance of guilt and protection.

chapters.title: The Fire Broadcast
chapters.summary: Dual timeline via tape recordings and Odile's present. We hear the 1974 broadcast: the Aldermoor choir mid-hymn when smoke fills the sanctuary, then the impossible—voices continuing calmly while screaming happens around them. The tape ends mid-note. Beat: the horror's shape revealed; survival was purchased.

chapters.title: Congregation of One
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She tracks down Father Ansel Brandt, the sole survivor of the 1974 choir, now ninety and living above a shuttered parish. He recognizes her face—she looks like her mother. He tells her the deal: the thing below took the choir in exchange for letting the congregation walk out of the fire. Beat: exposition as confession.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV, 1974. The choir's choice: the door would open outward only if someone sealed it behind them, choosing to be taken so the rest could live. Her mother, the soloist, was meant to stay—but slipped out at the last second, and the youngest alto, Ruthie, was pulled instead. Beat: the family wound exposed.

chapters.title: Return Policy
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The excavation crew starts vanishing—one found inside a locked supply closet, another simply absent, his radio still keyed and transmitting humming. City officials move to concrete over the door. Odile realizes sealing it without returning what was taken will just make it hungry elsewhere. Beat: false hope crushed.

chapters.title: The Listeners
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She goes on air and openly addresses the dead, asking what they want returned. For the first time they answer individually, not in unison: each names a piece of the song they never finished singing. They don't want freedom—they want completion. Beat: reframing the antagonist as the wronged.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Verse
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Researching the missing alto, she finds Ruthie Voss's sister, elderly, who has kept Ruthie's sheet music hidden fifty years, believing singing it aloud would call something. It contains the torn-out verse. The sister begs her to burn it. Beat: the key acquired at a cost of trust.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. He's been secretly recording Odile's shows, planning an exposé. Listening back, he hears a third voice in every silence—a low harmonic underneath everything, including his own speech. He tries to warn Odile and finds his mouth singing instead. Beat: the threat reaches the living; stakes go personal.

chapters.title: The Thing Below the Dial
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. On air, the harmonic speaks plainly through a caller: it was bound by song, fed by song, and the incomplete hymn left it starving and leaking. Give back the whole song or it will take a new choir—starting with everyone listening. Ratings spike. Beat: the bargain restated as ultimatum.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She learns the hymn from Ruthie's manuscript, practicing alone at night, discovering the final verse requires two voices in canon—call and answer. Her mother's tapes hold the answering line. She begins splicing them together. Beat: preparation, tenderness, and the growing sense she's being groomed to stay.

chapters.title: Brandt's Last Confession
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV, present day. Dying, he admits he helped seal the door in 1974—he pushed Ruthie toward it when her nerve broke. He gives Odile the chapel's original key and warns her: the door takes a substitute willingly given, or it takes freely. Beat: absolution refused; moral weight handed over.

chapters.title: Signal Lost
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. The station is condemned; power cut. But the transmitter keeps broadcasting on its own, airing the 1974 fire broadcast on loop. Marcus goes to shut it down manually and finds the studio full of wet footprints leading to the transmission booth, which shouldn't exist. Beat: the boundary between then and now dissolves.

chapters.title: The Door Remembers
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. At the excavation site at night, the sealed door stands exposed in the pit, and carved into it from the inside are tally marks—hundreds—counting days, then years, then stopping at a date Odile knows: her mother's death. Whatever was owed transferred to her bloodline. Beat: destiny made explicit; fear curdles into resolve.

chapters.title: Open Air
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She broadcasts the completed hymn live from the pit, Ruthie's verse and her mother's taped answer braided together. The door opens inward for the first time. Inside: the choir, unchanged since 1974, waiting mid-breath. They extend their hands—not menacing, pleading. Beat: climax begins; awe and terror fused.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The exchange demands a singer remain. Odile steps toward the threshold, ready to give herself, but the harmonic intervenes—it wants the debt-holder, not a volunteer, and her mother's escape in 1974 means the debt was never paid, only deferred. Beat: darkest moment; sacrifice seems both necessary and insufficient.

chapters.title: Answer Me
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She plays the final splice: her mother's voice, recorded decades ago, singing the answering line one last time—a message her mother left deliberately, knowing Odile would find it. The dead choir receives their song complete. The harmonic, fed at last, releases its claim. The choir crosses over singing. Beat: catharsis; love as the mechanism of salvation.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Outside
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She closes the door and seals it from the outside, carving her own single tally mark beside her mother's stopped count. The dead callers' voices fade one by one, each saying goodbye by name. Marcus arrives having heard everything on the transmitter; she lets him. Beat: grief and release intertwined.

chapters.title: A Smile for the Choir
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Odile's POV, months later. The station survives; her show changes—no more calls from the dead, just the living, lonelier and stranger than the dead ever were. On the anniversary night, the transmitter hums a single bar of the hymn, and Odile smiles and hums the answer. Beat: belonging redefined; peace earned, watched, and chosen.
